full_judgment:
Fazle Munim C.J:- This appeal arises out of First Misc. Appeal No. 163 of 1977 decided by a Bench of the High Court Division on November 14.19.80. 

 2. Respondent No. 1 instituted Title Suit No. 104 of 1974 in the court of 3rd Subordinate Judge, Dacca for filing the arbitration agreement under section 20 of the Arbitration Act. There was a contract, No. S/7/509/70-71 dated 9.2.71, between plaintiff-respondent No.1 and defendant No.2, namely, Director of Supply, Government of Pakistan, hereinafter referred to as "the buyer" for the supply of 57,50,000 B. Twill gunny-bags the consignee being Storage and Movement Officer (S&M. O.), Civil Supply Department (CSO) Halishaher, Chittagong and S&M.O. CSD. Khulna Plaintiff-respondent's case was that the goods under the contract were supplied to the nominated consignees on different dates. The buyer asked for encashment of Bank Guarantee No. 40 dated 18.2.71 and informed the plaintiff-respondent that only 75,000, pieces of gunny bags were so far received, by the S&M.O., CSD, Halishaher Chittagong. The plaintiff-respondent No. 1 was accordingly called upon to refund the excess amount which was already, paid to them. As, according to the contract, the plaintiff-respondent No 1 was to receive 95% of the price of goods despatched on production of Inspection Note of the Director of Supply and 5 % on production of receipt from the consignees, the plaintiff-respondent intimated him that no excess payment has been made to them and since they have fulfilled their part of the contract they were entitled to 5% of the price of goods supplied which amounted to Tk. 2,08,654.02. Further, the plaintiff-respondent No. 1 would invoke the arbitration clause of the contract if the buyer fails to make the payment as aforesaid. The buyer, respondent No. 2 neither made the payment nor agreed to the arbitration. The appellant which is the Government represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Commerce and Foreign Trade and respondent No. 2 the buyer, filed written statement stating that the plaintiff- respondent was not entitled to any amount whatsoever as they already withdrew the excess payment amounting Tk. 39,09,358.00 though the entire goods under the contract were not supplied to the consignees. The suit was, therefore, liable to be dismissed, and there was no question of filing the arbitration agreement in Court. The learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit on contest. After considering the respective claims of the parties concerned he referred to the point involved in the case, namely, whether the, arbitration agreement should be filed in Court. Reasons for his decision appeared from the following paragraph in his judgment: 

 “Plaintiff has instituted this suit for filing arbitration agreement before the court u/s 20 of the Arbitration Act. In the contract between the parties there is an arbitration clause to the effect that in the event of any question or dispute arising out of the contract the same shall be referred to an Arbitrator In the instant case, there is a dispute between, the parties about the supply of gunny bags by the plaintiff to the defendants. Plaintiff claims that he is entitled to get 5% price of the goods supplied to the defendants amounting to Taka 208,654.02. On the other hand, the defendants contention is that plaintiff drew excess payment of Tk. 39,09,358.00 without supplying the gunny bags per contract. He is, therefore, liable to make refund drawn by him in excess. It is, therefore, clear without any doubt that there is a dispute between the parties arising under the agreement. Therefore, this dispute should be referred to the Arbitrator as envisaged in-clause 21of the agreement between the parties. In the facts and circumstances of the case, I hold that provisions of section 20 of the Arbitration Act can be invoked  in the instant case." 

 3. Being aggrieved, the Government filed the aforesaid. First Miscellaneous Appeal in the High Court Division which upheld the decision of the trial court. It was ordered that the suit filed by the plaintiff-respondent may proceed in accordance with law and be disposed, of expeditiously. 

 "In the event of any question or disputes arising under these conditions or any special condition of contract or, in connection with the contract (except as to any matters the decision of which is specially provided for by these conditions) the same shall be referred to the award of an Arbitrator to be nominated by the purchaser and an Arbitrator to be nominated by the Contractor or in case of the said arbitrators not agreeing then to the award of an Umpire to be appointed by the Arbitrators in writing before proceeding on the reference and the decision of the Arbitrators or in the event of their not agreeing, of the Umpire appointed by them, shall be final and conclusive and the provisions of the Indian Arbitration Act, 1940 and of the Rules thereunder and any statutory modification thereof shall be deemed to supply to and be incorporated in this contract." 

 (2) The application shall be in writing and shall be numbered and registered as a miscellaneous case between one or more of the parties interested as applicant or applicants and the remainder as opposite party or opposite parties, if the application has been ,presented by all the parties, or, if otherwise, between the applicant and other parties. 

 (2A) A miscellaneous case registered under sub-section (2) shall, unless the Court considers it necessary to take any other evidence, ordinarily be disposed of on an affidavit." 

 8. Mr. A. W. Bhuiyan Deputy Attorney-General who appeared for the appellant submitted that in view of the express terms of clause 2 of the Agreement as amended upto date the respondents should have referred the matter of dispute, if any, to the sole arbitrator mentioned therein. In the absence of compliance with the terms of clause 21 of the Agreement there was no sufficient cause for filling the arbitration agreement in the Court, The suit filed by the respondents under section 20 of the Arbitration Act should, therefore, have been dismissed. The learned Deputy Attorney-General asserted that section 20 did not confer any jurisdiction upon the Court to order of the filing of arbitration agreement unless the provisions of that section are strictly complied with. One of the requirements is that sufficient cause must be shown for the exercise of jurisdiction by the Court under that section. He asserted that the respondent did not show why they did not take resort to clause 21 of the Agreement before filing the suit. In short, without first invoking the Arbitration clause provided in the agreement itself the plaintiff-respondents could not maintain the suit in question. He further submitted that since clause 21 of the Agreement expressly mentions that Secretary, Ministry of Industries as the sole Arbitrator in case of any dispute between the parties, the trial court was wrong in directing the parties to submit the names of arbitrators. This direction is in clear violation of the Arbitration clause. 

 9. Dr. Kamal Hossain, Counsel for the respondent, before making any submissions drew our attention to the following assertion made by the appellant in the written statement filed on behalf of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 "for arbitration the plaintiff should approach tile Secretary, Ministry of Commerce but they did not do so". The learned Counsel then showed that the Secretary, Ministry of Commerce and Foreign Trade is the defendant No.1. He submitted that in such circumstances the secretary of Commerce who is a party to the suit cannot sit to arbitrate. Besides, the Secretary, Ministry of Commerce is not mentioned as the Arbitrator in clause 21 of the Agreement. At this stage the learned Deputy Attorney-General intervened and submitted that there had been further amendment of clause 21 of the Agreement which now mentions, Secretary of Commerce as the arbitrator in case of Secretary, Ministry of Industries. It, however, so happens that at present both the Industries and Commerce Departments now consist of one Ministry, namely, Ministry of Industries and Commerce with two Secretaries, one in-charge of Industries and the other is in-charge of Commerce. Dr. Kamal Hossain, Counsel for the plaintiff respondent submitted that though Commerce and Industries now constitute one Ministry but their separateness is maintained by the appointment of a Secretary for each of the two Divisions, and there would be no difficulty in having the arbitration decided by the Secretary In-charge of the Industries Division. He also mentioned that amendment of the Arbitration clause even with regard to the name of designation of the Arbitrator which has been effected after the date of the contract should not affect the clause as existed on the date of the contract. 

 11. As to the scope of section 20 and the question of jurisdiction conferred on the Court. Dr. Kamal Hossain, referred to sub-section (4) of section 20 which empowers the Court to do the following; namely, (1) order the filing of the arbitration agreement in court (2) make reference to the arbitrator agreed upon by the parties, either in the agreement itself or being called upon by the Court and (3) appoint the arbitrator in case of the parties failure to agree upon any arbitrator. 

 12. The existence of the arbitration clause does not preclude the Court from ordering the filing of the agreement in Court. In support, he referred to the following observations of Hidayatullah, J. of the Indian Supreme Court in the case of Dhanrajamal Goblndram Vs. Shamji Kalidas and Co. reported in AIR 1951 SC 1285: 

 "The first is the judicial function to consider whether the arbitration agreement should be filed in Court or not. That may involve dealing with objections to the existence and validity of the agreement itself. Once that is done, and the Court has decided that the agreement must be filed, the first part of its powers and duties is over. It is significant that an appeal under s. 39 lies only against the decision on this part of sub-section (4). Then follow a ministerial act of reference to arbitrator or arbitrators appointed by the parties. That also was perfectly possible in this case, if the parties appointed the arbitrator or arbitrators. If the parties do not agree, the Court may be required to make a decision as to who should be selected as an arbitrator, and that may be a function either judicial, or procedural, or even ministerial but it is unnecessary to decide which it is." 

 13. He next referred to a case decided by the Lahore High Court reported in PLD 1952 Lahore 566. While discussing the scope of provisions of sub-section (4) of section 20 of the Arbitration Act, the learned Judge observed as follows: 

 14. Having regard to the provisions of section 20 of the Arbitration Act, particularly sub-section (4) thereof, it appears that the power of the Court to order the filing of the agreement in case the party opposing the filing fails to show sufficient cause has been expressly conferred. In the present case, the Deputy Attorney-General who appeared for the appellant could not show sufficient reasons against the filing of the agreement in Court. Nor such reasons were shown before the Courts below. The propriety regarding the appointment of arbitrator is, however, open to objection. Dr. Hossain submitted that the order of the trial court directing the parties to suggest the names of arbitrator within one month of the date of order was not justified either in fact or in law. Sub-section (4) of section 20 mentioned clearly the Court, after ordering the filing of agreement, "shall make an order of reference to the arbitrator appointed by the parties, whether in the agreement or otherwise." Clause 21 of the Agreement shows that an arbitrator has been appointed by the parties namely Secretary, Ministry of Industries. The question of the other eventuality mentioned in the sub-section does not, therefore, arise. Accordingly, the order of the trial court directing the parties to suggest the names of arbitrator within one month is uncalled for. The objection seems to be valid and reasonable. The second part of the trial court's order being not in conformity with the requirements of law as envisaged in sub-section (4) cannot, therefore, be sustained. Even after the amalgamation of the Ministries of Commerce and Industries, clause 21 can be given effect to, because the Department of Industries is still headed by a Secretary. The order that the agreement be filed in Court must, however, stand.
